content: The Socialist Patients' Collective (SPK), also referred to as the Patients' Front (PF), was a radical leftist group in Germany during the late 1960s and early 1970s. This group viewed medicine and doctors as adversaries of the patients' class and attributed illness to the effects of capitalism. They sought to use illness as a weapon to challenge and dismantle capitalist society. The SPK was officially established in February 1970 by Dr. Wolfgang Huber, a psychiatrist at Heidelberg University. The group emerged after Huber was dismissed from his position at the university clinic for refusing to cooperate with the psychiatric department. In response, his group therapy patients organized protests and even occupied the university's administrative offices. Huber warned the university's director that some of his patients might commit suicide if he was not allowed to continue working with them. As a result, he was reinstated with full pay and granted access to four rooms at the university. During their group therapy sessions, the SPK ostensibly discussed topics such as dialectics, Marxism, religion, education, and sexuality. However, in practice, their activities included training in explosives, radio transmission, photography, judo, and karate. On one occasion, Huber dismissed a mentally ill girl from the group, stating that after two weeks, she had shown no noticeable political progress. As parts of the group became increasingly militant, Huber was imprisoned in June 1971, leading to the eventual dissolution of the SPK. The group rebranded itself as the Information Center of the Red People's University (IZRU) and proposed the formation of guerrilla cells. However, many members soon joined the Red Army Faction, a prominent leftist terrorist organization. The SPK's ideology was rooted in the belief that the late-capitalist performance society of the Federal Republic of Germany was inherently sick, producing individuals who were physically or psychologically unwell. They argued that society could only be cured through revolution, including violent revolution if necessary. According to Jillian Becker, members of the SPK believed that curing their own mental disorders required violent attacks on society. They viewed their illnesses as tools to combat societal structures, despised doctors and capitalism, and identified them as enemies of the patient class. One of their slogans was: The system has made us sick. Let us strike the death blow to the sick system. Today, a group of individuals, including Ingeborg Muhler, a lawyer in Mannheim, claims to be the legal successors of the original SPK. They assert that they are the only pro-illness group in the world.
